name: Alabama
summary: Alabama offers tax incentives for data center development, but local pushback spread rapidly in mid-2026. Birmingham enacted a 6-month moratorium on large data centers (>20 MW) in March 2026, and in June 2026 Leeds, Homewood, Cullman, and Fort Payne each adopted their own data center moratoriums while reviewing zoning rules. The wave reached east-central Alabama in August 2026: Anniston adopted Resolution 26-R-97 on August 18 imposing a 12-month moratorium on data center permitting, development and licensing within its regulatory jurisdiction (with a Planning Commission study due in six months), and Westover's council unanimously passed a six-month moratorium the same night after residents opposed a proposed 437-acre project near Cheshire Drive. In early September 2026 Harpersville adopted a proactive six-month moratorium, and Fort Payne unanimously enacted an ordinance making data centers and battery storage conditional uses requiring zoning board review and public hearings while its moratorium runs through December 15. Foley joined the wave on September 14, 2026 with a six-month moratorium on data center, cryptocurrency-mining and server-farm applications while it updates water, air-pollution and noise ordinances.

name: Alaska
summary: No statewide data center legislation, but Anchorage has adopted preemptive zoning regulations requiring conditional use permits and setbacks for large data centers.

name: Arizona
summary: Arizona's statewide debate sharpened in September 2026: Attorney General Kris Mayes called for a statewide moratorium on new data center approvals, while Governor Katie Hobbs opposed a blanket pause; APS simultaneously proposed a 45% rate increase for data centers, citing grid constraints. On the local level, Pinal County supervisors voted 4-1 in the week of September 7-10, 2026 to reject Vermaland's 3,300-acre data center campus south of Eloy — which would have been Arizona's largest — even after the developer scaled it from 59 buildings and two gas plants down to 11 buildings and one. Tucson's 'Community Energy and Water Accountability' ordinance (enacted August 2026) remains the state's most prominent municipal restriction. Pima County's Board of Supervisors narrowly approved a 120-day moratorium on new data center projects in unincorporated areas on September 22, 2026, while it drafts code requirements that could include closed-loop cooling, noise reduction and design standards. Pima County's Planning and Zoning Commission voted 8-1 on October 28, 2026 to advance a conditional-use-permit requirement for data centers in heavy industrial zones, headed to the Board of Supervisors in early December. Oro Valley is moving toward a ban on data centers of 20 MW or more, and Gilbert postponed a vote on rules that would ban open-loop evaporative cooling and potable water for cooling, with a revised draft due December 15.

name: Arkansas
summary: Arkansas has no statewide moratorium or restriction legislation and still courts large projects, but county-level restriction spread rapidly in August 2026 and several of the pauses are among the longest in the country. Independence County's quorum court unanimously enacted a five-year moratorium on August 10, 2026 — running through 2031 — citing strain on local water supply despite having no specific project proposed. Madison County followed on August 17 with a unanimous 8-0 three-year moratorium, also with no known project in development; it is the second-longest pause in the state and one of five Arkansas counties with three-year or longer moratoriums. Union County and Carroll County each adopted one-year pauses in June 2026, and Russellville adopted a six-month moratorium in July. Central Arkansas has taken the regulatory route instead. The Pulaski County Quorum Court voted down a 12-month construction moratorium 10-3 on July 28, 2026 amid disputes over an exemption for the AVAIO Digital Wrightsville project, and a Little Rock moratorium proposal failed on a 4-4 deadlock on August 4. Both jurisdictions are instead writing rules: Little Rock passed regulations in June 2026, and on August 13 Pulaski County advanced an ordinance classifying large facilities as heavy industrial, requiring a conditional use permit, 500-foot residential setbacks and noise caps, but the ordinance drew an overflow crowd at the August 25 meeting and the final vote was delayed. Separately, a county judge dismissed a newspaper public-records suit seeking Google's utility rate contract for its $4 billion West Memphis data center, ruling the dispute belongs before the state Public Service Commission. North Little Rock's City Council approved an ordinance on September 15, 2026 restricting data center campuses to I-3 industrial zones under conditional use permits requiring demonstrated utility capacity. Pulaski County's Quorum Court passed its data center regulatory ordinance 11-4 on September 22, 2026, but County Judge Barry Hyde vetoed it on September 24; an override vote (requiring 9 of 15) is possible October 27. On October 20, 2026 Little Rock's board rejected a six-month data center moratorium on a 4-4 tie, its second failed moratorium attempt since August, as Google's $1 billion data center project advances.

name: California
summary: California now has the most comprehensive statewide data center laws in the nation. On September 21, 2026 Governor Newsom signed a seven-bill package — SB 1168 (McNerney), SB 886 (Padilla), SB 887, AB 1577, AB 2383, AB 2469 and AB 2619 — imposing reporting, infrastructure-cost and environmental requirements on data centers covering power, water and land use. SB 1168 directs the CPUC to ensure data centers pay for the transmission and distribution upgrades their load requires; SB 886 creates a separate electricity rate class for data centers; SB 887 requires environmental impact review. Local action continues to accelerate. Calexico's council voted 3-0 on September 16 to ban data centers via zoning code amendment — the third California city to do so. Tulare County extended its unincorporated-area moratorium by 10 months on a 5-0 vote on September 22 while it drafts permanent zoning rules (options include conditional use permits or an outright ban), and Oakland's City Council unanimously enacted a 45-day moratorium on October 6, 2026, effective immediately and extendable another 45 days while the city studies energy, water and public-health impacts. Mendocino County's supervisors voted 4-1 on October 6 to extend their urgency moratorium through August 21, 2028, exempting facilities under 3 MW. On September 15, San Francisco Supervisor Shamann Walton introduced an interim moratorium on new data centers, expansions and power upgrades — a first step toward permanent restrictions. Palm Springs extended its moratorium through August 25, 2028 on September 28, and Tulare County's supervisors adopted a formal position opposing data center development 3-2 on September 30. Earlier local restrictions remain in force across the Coachella Valley (Coachella's permanent ban, plus earlier bans in Perris and Desert Hot Springs), Imperial County (pause extended to a full year in July), Monterey Park (through January 2027), Indio, Escondido and Fresno, where the council voted 7-0 on September 3 to begin drafting a 10-year citywide ban. In Imperial County, the Superior Court issued a final ruling halting a nearly 1-million-square-foot data center complex because the county approved a lot merger without CEQA review; the developer has vowed to appeal. And after a Superior Court struck down Imperial County's moratorium in September, its Board of Supervisors unanimously reinstated a temporary emergency moratorium on October 6, 2026, while weighing a possible special election on data center limits. In mid-October the wave reached San Francisco: the Board of Supervisors unanimously passed Walton's interim moratorium on October 13, 2026, and Mayor Daniel Lurie signed it on October 16 — a 45-day citywide pause on new data center approvals, extendable to roughly 22 months, that halts a NOVVA project in Bayview and a 49.5 MW Dogpatch building. Richmond's 45-day urgency moratorium (Ordinance No. 13-26 N.S., adopted September 15) runs through October 30, with an October 20 hearing on a 22-month-and-15-day extension. In mid-to-late October 2026, Gilroy extended its moratorium by over ten months (exempting the $2B AWS facility under construction), Hawthorne extended its moratorium through September 2027, and San Mateo County supervisors began evaluating zoning limits for unincorporated areas after dropping a proposed countywide ban. In late October the wave reached the state's second-largest city: San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria signed Executive Order 2026-2 on October 22, 2026 directing a temporary moratorium on new data centers, and the City Council unanimously ratified the 45-day pause on October 27 — a response to a reported 400 MW proposal at the Navy's NAVWAR site. In the Bay Area, Pittsburg's council unanimously adopted a 45-day moratorium aimed at the next two phases of the AVAIO project at the former Delta View Golf Course. On November 3, 2026, Alhambra voters approved a citywide data center ban with ~83% support — the first voter-enacted municipal ban in California — while Whittier adopted a 45-day urgency moratorium on data center permits (extendable at a December 8 hearing) and El Segundo extended its moratorium into September 2027.

name: Colorado
summary: No statewide moratorium. Denver City Council voted unanimously on May 18, 2026 to enact a one-year moratorium on new data center zoning permits and site development plans, prompted by Stage 1 drought conditions and Denver Water's call for a 20% reduction; already-permitted work is exempt (CoreSite's DE3 is grandfathered while two additional planned buildings are halted), and the city is forming a task force. Larimer County has an active moratorium, Logan County enacted and lifted one after passing regulations, and Weld County adopted new zoning requirements. On July 7, 2026 the City and County of Broomfield unanimously approved an 18-month moratorium (through December 2027) on data centers using 10 MW or more. Colorado Springs' Planning Commission approved Project Taurus 6-2 on August 3, 2026 with conditions including a 50 MW cap and a requirement that utility data be published; an appeal was filed and the City Council is expected to decide in September. Mead's trustees added a 12-month moratorium on a 4-2 vote on August 31, 2026, to study infrastructure, water use and setbacks before accepting applications. Colorado Springs' council voted 7-2 on September 17, 2026 to postpone a decision on the Project Taurus data center appeal to April 2027 pending a utilities contract and citywide data center rules, and Moffat County commissioners postponed a vote on a proposed six-to-twelve-month moratorium to October 13 to gather public input. Aurora's City Council scheduled a November 2, 2026 vote on an indefinite data center moratorium — requiring seven votes to pass and exempting the already-approved Trident project.

name: Connecticut
summary: Connecticut's SB 43 to update data center tax credits (5-year minimum use period) remains in committee. In the week of September 7-10, 2026, Governor Ned Lamont declared that Connecticut 'will not host massive AI data centers,' citing concern that their electricity consumption could raise utility rates; he said smaller projects with self-supplied power and local approval would still be permitted. The state's 2021 data center tax incentive program had drawn minimal interest. In Ellington, the Planning and Zoning Commission postponed its public hearing on a proposed one-year moratorium on data centers and battery energy storage systems to November 23, 2026. Cromwell's Planning and Zoning Commission revived a proposed six-month moratorium in early November 2026 — after an initial version failed and emails surfaced showing town officials had discussed a Geer Street data center project with developer Global Common for over a year — with a public hearing set for December 3, 2026. Ellington continues drafting its own one-year moratorium on large-scale data centers.

name: Delaware
summary: No statewide moratorium legislation, but New Castle County enacted comprehensive data center zoning regulations and DNREC denied a major data center under the Coastal Zone Act. On August 18, 2026 Harrington's council unanimously rejected an ordinance that would have allowed data centers as a conditional use, with residents citing water, sewer, electrical infrastructure and noise impacts. In a first for Delaware, Dover’s City Council unanimously approved an 18-month moratorium on data center construction in mid-October 2026, pausing reviews of large energy-use facilities (including those over 30 MW) while the city writes permanent rules; one councilman called for an outright ban. No application had been filed in the city.

name: Florida
summary: Governor Ron DeSantis signed SB 484 — the Florida Hyperscale Data Center Act — into law on May 7, 2026 (effective July 1). The law classifies data centers consuming 50+ MW at peak demand as 'large-scale,' bars utilities from passing data center costs onto residential and small-business ratepayers, requires data centers to pay their full cost of service, creates a permitting framework to protect aquifers and local water (mandating reclaimed water where feasible), and preserves local government authority to deny or impose stricter standards on data center projects. Florida continues to attract data center investment, particularly in the Miami and Jacksonville markets, but local pushback emerged in mid-2026: Sarasota County adopted a one-year hyperscale moratorium in July, DeSoto County moved toward one, and Lakeland approved a one-year moratorium on first reading July 21, 2026 (final reading August 3). Governor DeSantis was one of only three governors — along with New Hampshire's Ayotte and Vermont's Scott — who declined to sign the White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge expanded on July 23, 2026. Local restriction widened in August 2026. Washington County's commissioners unanimously approved a one-year moratorium on August 20 halting acceptance, processing, review and approval of data center applications in unincorporated areas, exempting only facilities where computer equipment occupies no more than 5% of gross floor area with demand under 250 kW. In Palm Beach County, commissioners voted 5-1 in July to reject Project Tango — a $2 billion AI campus — without prejudice after water-demand estimates diverged sharply between the developer's 5,000-gallon daily figure and county staff's 100,000-gallon projection, and approved a temporary halt on large-scale applications that went to a public hearing on August 27. Late August brought the first regulatory test of SB 484: the Public Service Commission is reviewing Duke Energy's first large-load proposal under the law, weighing whether it adequately shields ratepayers from data center costs, with a written order expected after post-hearing briefs. Martin County commissioners voted 4-1 on August 27 to put a moratorium discussion on their next agenda, while Tallahassee commissioners rejected a proposed AI data center ban 3-2 the same day, noting existing zoning already excludes such facilities. In early September 2026 Indiantown's Village Council rejected a proposed hyperscale application pause 4-1 — firing the village manager and removing the village attorney the same night — while North Port scheduled a moratorium vote for September 8. In September 2026, Levy County unanimously approved a moratorium in unincorporated areas (Ordinance 2026-05, through September 30, 2027), and an Orange County commissioner proposed a one-year moratorium on AI data center applications citing projected groundwater shortfalls. Manatee County commissioners unanimously enacted a 12-month moratorium on September 15, 2026; Alachua County's planning commission approved a 12-month moratorium the same day; and Leon County commissioners advanced an 18-month moratorium toward a final vote on October 13. The week of September 21, 2026 brought further restrictions: Wakulla County unanimously adopted an outright ban on data centers in unincorporated areas on September 22, and North Port approved an 18-month moratorium 3-2 on September 23 (exempting a roughly 900,000-square-foot project already proposed). Marion County had approved a 12-month moratorium on data centers of 50 MW or more on September 15. Edgewater's City Council unanimously enacted a permanent ban on data centers, AI data centers and crypto mining on September 14, 2026, with a November 3 ballot measure (Charter Amendment 4) to write the ban into the city charter. Volusia County's Council gave final approval on October 20, 2026 to a permanent ban on large-scale data centers in unincorporated areas, one of the first permanent county-level bans in the country. On October 13, 2026 Lake County commissioners voted 3-2 to postpone public hearings on proposed large-scale data center rules and asked staff to draft a 90-day extension of the county’s moratorium, which expires in December; Broward County commissioner Lamar Fisher asked staff to draft a one-year moratorium for unincorporated areas (on the October 20 agenda); and Martin County advanced its one-year moratorium at the first of two hearings, with the final hearing set for October 27. In the week of October 19, 2026, Gilchrist County enacted a one-year AI data center moratorium, Broward County voted unanimously to begin drafting a one-year moratorium for unincorporated areas, Dade City advanced a 12-month pause on first reading over water concerns, and Edgewater advanced a proposal toward a permanent ban with a final vote expected in November. Martin County's moratorium took effect in late October 2026, though a previously submitted application may proceed under prior rules, and DeSoto County commissioners deadlocked 2-2 on — and thereby rejected — a DCIP Group rezoning of about 238 acres for a data center campus. In the first week of November 2026, Edgewater voters ratified the city's data center ban by charter amendment (~77% yes on Amendment 4, November 3), and the Public Service Commission rejected Duke Energy Florida's proposed large-load tariff — the first contested test of SB 484 — finding the proposal excluded some qualifying large-load customers and lacked evidence that each would cover its full cost of service; Duke must refile. Broward County's one-year moratorium for unincorporated areas is being drafted with a final vote expected in November or December.

name: Georgia
summary: All statewide data center bills (HB 1012 moratorium, SB 408 and SB 410 tax exemption repeal) failed when the 2026 legislative session ended. Local momentum continues: Camden County's Board of Commissioners voted on May 5, 2026 to adopt a six-month moratorium (the first on Georgia's coast) amid a contested industrial-park rezoning push, and Lee County commissioners weighed extending their existing moratorium in late May. Local action continued through July 2026: Walker County adopted a 30-day application moratorium on July 10 with a 180-day extension pending an August 6 hearing, Marietta adopted a temporary moratorium through December 31, and DeKalb County extended its pause into early 2027. Multiple counties in central/west Georgia retain active moratoriums including DeKalb, Pike, Lamar, Troup counties and the City of LaGrange. Atlanta requires special use permits within the Beltline radius. Cherokee County joined on July 22, 2026 with a 30-day moratorium that commissioners plan to extend into early 2027, and residents in Dalton — which third-party data shows has the highest documented data center count in its region — are organizing for a pause over the county administrator's objection. Governor Brian Kemp was among the 23 Republican governors who signed the White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge on July 23, 2026. Albany adopted a 12-month moratorium in early August 2026. On August 13 the Marietta City Council voted 5-2 to approve an 11-acre data center despite the city's own six-month moratorium, because developer Prime Group Holdings' application predated the pause; dozens of residents protested. Montgomery County gave first reading to a strict ordinance requiring a 1,500-foot buffer, a three-mile separation from water bodies and farmland, and a no-tax-abatement pledge. Development also continues at scale: on August 3 Effingham County approved OpenAI's Project Camellia, a $20 billion, 1,440-acre campus with a 50% property tax abatement for 15 years and $32 million for local schools. A Maysville City Council meeting was adjourned after 14 minutes on August 3 when an update on the Northern Data/Rumble project drew shouting from the audience. Early September 2026 brought further local action: Forest Park approved a 90-day moratorium to draft zoning rules, Dougherty County unanimously extended its moratorium another 180 days on August 31, and Bulloch County commissioners rejected a permanent ban 4-3 while keeping their existing moratorium through the end of 2026. In late September 2026 Lovejoy banned data center construction citywide (September 29) after opposition to a proposed 3.5-million-square-foot campus near schools, and Jesup gave first reading 4-2 to an ordinance restricting data centers to conditional uses in light industrial zones. Stephens County commissioners unanimously extended their land-use application moratorium to January 14, 2027 on October 13, 2026, the second extension of a pause begun in April. Jefferson County's commission passed a technology zoning ordinance covering data centers in late October 2026; with no land yet zoned for the new district, any project will require a full rezoning with multiple public meetings.

name: Hawaii
summary: No known data center moratorium or restriction legislation.

name: Idaho
summary: No statewide data center legislation, but Kootenai County enacted a moratorium (now expired, replaced by permanent aquifer protections) and Ada County is developing data center zoning amendments. Governor Brad Little joined President Trump at the July 23, 2026 White House roundtable expanding the Ratepayer Protection Pledge.

name: Illinois
summary: HB 4172 (three-month moratorium) stalled in committee. On June 5, 2026 Governor Pritzker formally directed DCEO to pause processing new Data Center Investment Program agreements starting July 1, 2026 (a two-year administrative suspension; existing agreements are honored), and released a seven-point reform framework urging the legislature to act. The POWER Act (HB 5513/SB 4016) — which would shift grid costs to data centers, incentivize clean energy, and limit water use — did not pass before the May 31, 2026 adjournment; the DCEO suspension took effect on schedule July 1, 2026 and Pritzker is pressing for action in the fall veto session. Litigation has become a factor: residents sued on July 31, 2026 over an $18 billion, 472-acre campus in Grayslake, alleging improper private discussions violated the state's Open Meetings Act and seeking to void the 2024-2025 approvals and halt further permits. In September 2026, Lake County adopted an eight-month moratorium on unincorporated-area data center development after receiving more than 1,200 public comments. Normal's Town Council voted 6-1 on September 21, 2026 to extend its moratorium through May 31, 2027 pending possible state legislation, and Galesburg gave first reading to a 180-day moratorium the same week. Evanston determined in late September 2026 that its zoning code does not currently permit data centers — a de facto moratorium — and is evaluating a formal pause, while Mahomet opened preliminary talks with Clean Cloud Energy over a potential project. Tazewell County's board unanimously approved a nine-month countywide moratorium on data center applications on October 28, 2026, running to July 28, 2027, while the county drafts a data center ordinance. On November 3, 2026, Illinois voters weighed in through seven non-binding advisory questions, all breaking against data centers: Bloomington voters backed a moratorium advisory with ~78% and Morgan County voters backed a restriction advisory with ~88%, while pro-data-center advisory measures failed in Joliet (~79% opposed) and in Madison County's Chouteau, Granite City, Nameoki and Venice townships (74-83% opposed).

name: Indiana
summary: Indiana HB 1333 passed the House 54-45 (February 2026) but stalled in the Senate Utilities Committee; the controversial 'permitted use' farmland provision was explicitly rejected. The core 1% revenue-sharing provision was folded into HB 1210, which was enacted into law. On May 4-14, 2026 the Indianapolis City-County Council unanimously passed a non-binding resolution (Proposal 158) urging the Metropolitan Development Commission to pause data center approvals until May 7, 2027 or until tighter rules are adopted; the MDC is expected to discuss draft special development standards at its June 3, 2026 meeting. In mid-July 2026 an Indianapolis City-County Council committee approved a binding moratorium on new data center approvals through December 31, 2027, and Valparaiso's council advanced its own moratorium ordinance. The Indianapolis pause became binding on August 10, 2026, when the City-County Council voted 23-1 to bar new data center construction in Marion County through the end of 2027, giving councilors time to finalize noise, water management and electrical capacity rules; the Metropolitan Development Commission ratified it on August 19. Three previously approved projects — DC Blox in Warren Township, Metrobloks in Martindale-Brightwood, and Sabey in Decatur Township — are unaffected. Elkhart County held a first reading on August 18 of a moratorium covering data centers and battery storage running to December 31, 2027, with a special meeting for public comment and a vote on August 27. In St. Joseph County, a vote on expanding the AM General TIF district to include a Microsoft data center — which would let the county borrow up to $4 million — was postponed to September 22 amid questions about tax revenue distribution. Nearly a third of Indiana counties have now moved to restrict data centers. The City of Elkhart's council voted 9-0 on August 27, 2026 to stop accepting data center and battery storage applications until December 2027 while it studies grid, water, safety, traffic and noise impacts — a pause that covers only the city, with the separate county-level moratorium still pending. In Kokomo, the Plan Commission backed a zoning amendment 5-1 on August 17 that would allow data centers on industrial land, with a Common Council vote expected in September. In Fort Wayne, a one-year pause on council data center actions was introduced in September 2026 with unanimous support for introduction. Zionsville's Town Council approved a one-year moratorium (also covering solar, wind and battery storage) on September 21, 2026; Owen County commissioners unanimously approved a one-year moratorium on September 22; and Fort Wayne's council vote on its proposed one-year pause was delayed to October 13 amid multiple amendments. On October 13, 2026 Fort Wayne’s City Council defeated the proposed one-year data center moratorium on a 4-4 tie and rejected a data center task force resolution 5-3. Warrick County is advancing a permanent Data Center Overlay district with noise caps, setbacks and water limits ahead of November public hearings, driven by Alcoa's ~700-acre Project Alloy. A WFYI tally reported October 21, 2026 that more than half of Indiana counties now restrict data centers: 32 county moratoriums, 14 regulatory ordinances and 4 explicit bans.

name: Iowa
summary: No statewide moratorium, but Iowa has significant local action. Clarke and Johnson counties enacted moratoriums, Linn County passed one of the nation's strictest data center zoning ordinances with 1,000-foot setbacks and water study requirements, and Dubuque County supervisors approved a 12-month moratorium on May 26, 2026. Johnson County is now advancing what would be among the region's strictest data center ordinances — including closed-loop cooling requirements and designated development areas — despite having no active project applications; officials describe the intent as discouraging rather than banning facilities. On August 19, 2026 Maquoketa ended preliminary discussions with developer Gronen over a facility at the South Highway 61 Industrial Park, clarifying that no nondisclosure agreements had been signed, and said it will review its Heavy Industrial District regulations governing future data center development. Salix's council rejected a one-year moratorium 3-2 on August 21 after Google was revealed as the developer behind a local project, and Cedar Rapids announced housing incentives on August 27 to absorb the influx of data center construction workers. Marshall County supervisors unanimously approved a six-month, extendable moratorium on September 23, 2026 covering data centers, AI computing, data mining and cryptocurrency operations. Sioux County held a public hearing September 28, 2026 on a data center ordinance with heightened standards (readings set for October 13 and 27), and Center Point began drafting its own ordinance modeled on neighboring counties. Poweshiek County supervisors passed a 12-month moratorium (Resolution 2027-11, 2-1 vote) on September 28, 2026, effective until permanent zoning is adopted, and Fort Madison tabled its draft 'High Infrastructure Impact Development' ordinance for another month in early November.

name: Kansas
summary: No statewide data center legislation, but Kansas local action accelerated sharply in July 2026. Lawrence city commissioners unanimously adopted a two-year moratorium on large-scale data centers on July 14, 2026 — doubling an originally proposed one-year pause — while staff study long-term code changes. Lyon County commissioners approved a six-month moratorium on July 23, 2026 covering data centers and battery energy storage (through January 22, 2027), alongside a separate solar moratorium expiring December 1, 2026. Emporia took the opposite tack on July 22, 2026, approving three ordinances creating a digital infrastructure district with zoning protections; a citizen petition to prohibit data centers outright was not acted on and could reach the November 2026 ballot. Sedgwick County and Harvey County retain earlier moratoriums and Miami County has considered a one-to-two-year pause. Franklin County adopted a moratorium on data center planning and construction on September 2, 2026, running until December 31, 2028. Marysville adopted a 12-month moratorium in mid-September 2026, defining data centers broadly (hyperscale, cloud, AI and crypto) while its planning commission reviews zoning amendments. Butler County commissioners unanimously delayed action on proposed data center siting, noise, lighting, water and decommissioning regulations on October 6, 2026, revisiting them October 27. Hutchinson is drafting data center rules with 60 dB daytime / 50 dB nighttime noise caps at the property line, with a planning commission hearing November 10 and council action expected December 1, 2026. On November 3, 2026 Kansas voters in three cities enacted outright bans: El Dorado approved a citizen initiative banning high-impact data centers and large battery storage with 71.5% (2,966-1,183), Ottawa banned data centers above 25 MW with ~72%, and Emporia — whose measure reached the ballot only by court order, with a validation suit still pending — approved a ban on high-impact facilities with ~60%, cutting against the city council's 2026 digital-infrastructure-district strategy. Combined with the active county and city moratoriums in Sedgwick, Harvey, Franklin, Lyon, Lawrence and Marysville, Kansas now has substantial enacted local restrictions despite no statewide legislation.

name: Kentucky
summary: Kentucky has no statewide data center moratorium and continues to court large projects, but its largest city has now paused new development. Louisville Metro Council voted 24-1 on August 13, 2026 to adopt a six-month moratorium blocking planners from approving new data center proposals until the council adopts comprehensive zoning rules, after the Planning and Zoning Committee advanced it 7-1 on August 4. Protesters at the vote pressed for a full year. The pause is meant to give the council time to study energy and water demand, infrastructure needs, tax implications and neighborhood noise; on August 20 the Louisville Planning Commission moved to strengthen the underlying restrictions. Nicholasville passed its own six-month moratorium on August 11, with residents citing electric bills, property taxes and water. Local restriction now spans a dozen Kentucky jurisdictions. Separately, a planned Paducah campus has been caught up in a proposed federal ban on AI data centers on certain federal land. The wave continued into September 2026: Rowan County's Fiscal Court approved a two-year moratorium on large-scale data centers (the county lacks zoning and will study a conditional-use process), and Winchester's commissioners unanimously passed a one-year moratorium within city limits. On September 14, 2026 Woodford County's fiscal court unanimously approved a permanent ban on data center construction — reported as the first Kentucky county to permanently ban data centers. In late September 2026, Mercer County's fiscal court unanimously rejected proposed hyperscale zoning regulations near the E.W. Brown Generating Station (its one-year moratorium remains in effect), Scott County extended its moratorium, and Georgetown's City Council voted unanimously on September 30 to direct counsel to draft a ban on hyperscale 'mega' facilities. Lexington's Urban County Council pause on data center permits, development plans and zone changes (enacted June 9, 2026) runs through October 31, 2026, with an extension receiving first reading on October 8, 2026 and draft zoning rules out for public comment. In October 2026 Lexington's Urban County Council extended the moratorium through October 2027 and unanimously adopted a zoning text amendment banning data centers over 50,000 square feet, capping energy use at 25 MW and limiting noise. Separately, on October 13, 2026 Mason County's Fiscal Court voted unanimously to approve a development contract for an approximately $15 billion Meta hyperscale campus (about 2,000 construction and 400 permanent jobs), with work required to begin within three years. Calloway County's Fiscal Court approved a one-year moratorium on new data centers and expansions 4-1 on October 21, 2026. Georgetown's council unanimously extended its data center moratorium a second time, through June 30, 2027, the week of October 26, 2026, while it drafts a citywide ban on hyperscale facilities.

name: Louisiana
summary: No statewide moratorium legislation, but New Orleans enacted a one-year citywide ban on data center construction in January 2026. Louisiana continues to attract major data center investment in northern parishes. Governor Jeff Landry joined President Trump at the July 23, 2026 White House roundtable expanding the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, which commits signatories to keeping data center infrastructure and generation costs off other utility customers. On August 13, 2026 the Louisiana Public Service Commission voted 3-1 to let Meta keep details of its Richland Parish data center confidential, overruling an administrative law judge's subpoena for job and energy-use data; a trial on Entergy's $13 billion power plant expansion is set for October with a decision expected in December. On August 18 a Caddo Parish commissioner proposed a two-year moratorium on tax incentives for data centers, referred to the special projects committee — though the parish attorney noted state law requires a master plan before a moratorium can be adopted. Ascension Parish's council approved a 90-day data center moratorium without objection on October 26, 2026, with the matter returning to the council on January 21, 2027.

name: Maine
summary: On April 29, 2026, Maine's Legislature failed to override Governor Mills' veto of LD 307 — the House voted 72-65 and the Senate 20-11, both falling short of the two-thirds majority required. The decisive defeat ends the path for what would have been the first statewide data center moratorium in US history. Mills had vetoed LD 307 on April 24 because it lacked an exemption for the planned Jay data center at the former Androscoggin Mill site. She separately signed LD 713 (banning data centers from Maine's business development tax incentive programs) and on April 29, 2026 issued Executive Order 5 establishing the 15-member Maine Data Center Advisory Council, which is due to deliver recommendations by January 29, 2027. Local moratoria remain active in Bangor and other communities; Scarborough and Brunswick each enacted 180-day moratoria in early June 2026, and Warren voters approved one on July 8. The veto override defeat has prompted national reflection in moratorium-curious states. On August 27, 2026 Eastport's Planning Board unanimously recommended a permanent ban on data centers across all of the city's zoning districts, sending the question to the city council. In September 2026, Gorham sent a proposed permanent data center ban to its planning board, and Eastport held a public hearing on citizen-initiated ordinances targeting a proposed underwater AI data center in Western Passage. Old Town's council unanimously enacted a six-month moratorium on data centers in industrial zones on October 5, 2026, retroactive to September 8. Local restrictions hardened into permanent bans in early November 2026. On November 3, voters in four Maine towns approved restrictions: North Berwick banned data centers above 25,000 square feet (~78%), while Wiscasset (~66%), Peru (~76%) and Wells (~82%) each adopted 180-day or six-month moratoriums. On November 4, Scarborough's Town Council unanimously prohibited data centers in all zoning districts — converting its June moratorium into a permanent ban after its Sustainability Committee concluded the drawbacks outweigh the benefits — and Westbrook's City Council unanimously banned standalone data centers the same week, removing them from the Rock Row Contract Zone, the only zone that had permitted them. With multiple enacted municipal bans now in force, Maine has moved from discussion to active local restrictions despite the failed statewide moratorium.

name: Maryland
summary: Maryland HB 120 (data center construction moratorium unless co-located with generation) died in committee when the General Assembly adjourned in early April 2026, but county governments have made Maryland one of the most restricted states in the country. Howard County unanimously passed CB31-2026 — the S.M.A.R.T. Siting Act — on June 1, 2026, halting new data center development through November 2, 2027 and creating a study task force. Prince George's County enacted a two-year pause on hyperscale development on July 7, 2026 (liftable early if a zoning framework is adopted). On May 11, 2026 the Baltimore City Council passed Bill 26-0158, a one-year moratorium on data centers using 10 MW or more plus a nine-month impact study. On July 22, 2026 Montgomery County Council committees voted unanimously to merge two competing bills into a single 18-month moratorium and send it to the full council, building on County Executive Elrich's six-month executive-order pause from June. Baltimore County and Frederick County restrictions also remain in place. Prince George's County extended its hyperscale pause in early August 2026. On August 9, Amazon withdrew a planned campus near the Calvert Cliffs Nuclear Power Plant, citing internal infrastructure planning rather than local opposition; Calvert County is pursuing a six-month moratorium regardless. On September 22, 2026 the Baltimore County Council voted unanimously to extend its data center moratorium through the end of 2027, citing insufficient industry responses on environmental impact and energy costs. Washington County's commissioners approved a 12-month moratorium on data center applications in unincorporated areas on June 30, 2026, and announced in late September a regulatory timeline extending through a June 2027 public hearing. On October 5, 2026 the Anne Arundel County Council voted 7-0 to enact an amended Bill 63-26 imposing a moratorium on new data centers through January 31, 2028 — or until comprehensive legislation is adopted — replacing an earlier proposal for an outright ban. Frederick County's moratorium — in force to July 1, 2027 — survived its first courtroom test in late October 2026 when a judge denied Quantum Maryland's request for a temporary restraining order; a preliminary injunction hearing is set for November 10.

name: Massachusetts
summary: Massachusetts imposed statewide restrictions by executive action. On September 8, 2026 Governor Maura Healey signed an executive order requiring proposed data centers with peak electricity demand above 25 MW to obtain local approval before state permitting can advance: developers must show they meet the state's Data Center Framework and file a community benefits agreement with the host community. The order also bars state agencies from signing NDAs with data center developers and directs MassDEP to establish, by the end of 2026, an 'alternative compliance payment' for data centers that fail to produce enough new clean electricity to cover their consumption, feeding a new Ratepayer Protection Fund. The order follows the administration's earlier halt of data center tax breaks. In Boston, Councilor Miniard Culpepper introduced a zoning amendment on September 16, 2026 to ban new data center construction citywide — the definition covers AI, cryptocurrency mining and cloud computing facilities; the city has 43 existing facilities. Local pauses continue to accumulate: Westfield's City Council gave final unanimous approval to a 12-month moratorium on July 6, 2026, joining earlier action in Lowell, Everett, and Shutesbury. Taunton's Municipal Council unanimously enacted a 365-day data center moratorium on October 20, 2026, declining a developer's request to exempt a proposed 24 MW facility.

name: Michigan
summary: Michigan introduced a bipartisan House bill package (HB 5594-5596) proposing a one-year moratorium preventing EGLE and local governments from issuing data center permits until April 2027. Governor Whitmer has explicitly stated she would veto any moratorium legislation, calling it 'an automatic non-starter.' More than 20 Michigan townships and cities have enacted local moratoria independently — the most of any state — with Meridian Township, Macomb County's Washington Township, and the City of Flint (a one-year pause on June 8, 2026) among the most recent. In June 2026 legislators renewed the statewide push: HB 5594-5596 (House) and companion SB 1018-1020 (Senate) were introduced to halt data center development until April 1, 2027, and Senate Democrats unveiled a separate eight-bill regulatory package — though none has been enacted. On July 15, 2026 Governor Whitmer unveiled the Michigan Affordable and Responsible Growth Action Plan, pairing a call for lawmakers to codify consumer and energy-cost guardrails in statute with a voluntary industry pledge — residents never pay for data center energy demand, companies build or buy additional energy resources, grid reliability and freshwater protection commitments, and jobs and community benefits. Google and Oracle announced support the same day. Whitmer continues to oppose a statewide moratorium. Kalamazoo's City Commission approved a resolution on August 18, 2026 enacting a one-year data center moratorium, with the community divided over whether the temporary pause should become a permanent ban. Bay City's planning commission formed a subcommittee on August 20 to study a draft ordinance addressing facility size, power demand, water use, noise and decommissioning, with a revisit scheduled for October. Garfield Charter Township (Grand Traverse County) unanimously adopted a one-year moratorium on data centers and crypto mining on August 25, 2026, extendable to 18 months, to study water and power impacts. Wixom ended its six-month moratorium early in September 2026 and replaced it with stricter zoning — a 1,500-foot setback from homes, schools and parks, a well-water ban and mandatory sound studies — as developer Wixom Industrial One LLC pressed a federal lawsuit over the pause. In September 2026, Zeeland Township adopted a one-year moratorium on data centers and energy facilities during its master plan update. Kalamazoo scheduled a public hearing in late September 2026 to convert its moratorium resolution into an enforceable zoning amendment. Saginaw's City Council unanimously adopted a permanent zoning ordinance on September 28, 2026 classifying data centers as special land uses with a 500-foot residential setback, effective October 9. Alpena County's Board of Commissioners approved a non-binding resolution (reported November 1, 2026) urging Northeast Michigan local governments to adopt data center moratoriums and transparency requirements, though the county itself has no zoning jurisdiction over such projects.

name: Minnesota
summary: Minnesota enacted SF 608 (June 2025) restricting enterprise data centers to industrial districts statewide. The 2026 statewide moratorium bills (HF 4888 and SF 4298) died when the Legislature adjourned sine die on May 18, 2026 without either receiving a committee hearing. Local action accelerated: on May 21, 2026 the Minneapolis City Council voted 8-5 to enact a six-month interim moratorium on data centers larger than 350,000 sq ft (the downtown core is exempt), giving final approval on June 25. Inver Grove Heights approved its own one-year moratorium on June 26, 2026 despite a developer's litigation threat, while Eagan — the first Minnesota city to enact a data center moratorium — was sued on June 15 by a developer seeking to void its pause. North Mankato is refining a moratorium targeting facilities over 150,000 square feet or using 50,000 or more gallons of water daily, with a second public hearing and council vote pending as of August 18, 2026. In mid-September 2026, Woodbury staff drafted a one-year interim moratorium headed to its City Council on September 23, and Harmony advanced an ordinance requiring closed-loop cooling, a 60,000-gallon-per-month cooling water cap, annual noise studies and a prohibition on NDAs. North Mankato adopted its one-year moratorium on September 22, 2026, and Woodbury's City Council approved an up-to-one-year interim moratorium on September 23, grandfathering three existing facilities. In Pine Island, a court order halted a proposed data center project pending a legal challenge, with the next hearing set for November 16, 2026. Northfield's council unanimously approved a 200-foot data center setback from existing and planned trails on October 6, 2026. Harmony's Planning and Zoning Commission approved the sixth draft of its data center ordinance on October 28, 2026, sending it to a City Council vote on November 10. Caledonia adopted a 12-month moratorium (Ordinance 2026-02) on October 26, 2026 while its planning commission drafts zoning. Not every community is pausing: Hermantown's City Council unanimously approved Google's proposed data center on October 30, 2026, despite 55 of 60 public speakers opposing it.

name: Mississippi
summary: Mississippi offers tax incentives to attract data center development, including property tax exemptions for qualifying facilities, and has drawn major projects including xAI's Southaven retrofit. Local resistance emerged in July 2026: on July 14, 2026 the Jackson City Council voted 5-2 for a 183-day moratorium on data centers — the first in the state — with members saying the capital is 'not ready for a data center.' In Warren County, residents have rallied against a proposed Amazon data center near Vicksburg, citing noise, pollution, utility costs, and its proximity to an elementary school.

name: Missouri
summary: No statewide moratorium legislation, but Missouri is a hotbed of local action. St. Charles enacted a citywide moratorium and is considering a permanent ban. Kansas City and St. Louis enacted zoning restrictions, and Columbia froze permits. Jackson County passed a 180-day moratorium (8-0) on June 22, 2026, and Springfield followed with a 120-day administrative delay on June 29. In mid-July 2026 the pace picked up again: St. Charles County unanimously approved a six-month moratorium on July 13 and the City of St. Joseph paused new applications the same day. Missouri also landed two of the nation's largest 2026 data center announcements — a $15B Google campus and a $10B Amazon campus, both in Montgomery County. Kansas City is now reviewing a 20-story downtown data center that would redevelop the historic Western Newspaper Union building; more than 80 residents turned out against it over water demand and preservation concerns, and the City Planning Commission takes it up August 5, 2026. On August 12, 2026 state lawmakers announced plans for AI and data center legislation when the General Assembly reconvenes in January 2027, and released an evaluation framework for local governments assessing proposals. Local decisions continue to cut both ways: St. Joseph's council rejected a proposal to create a citizen data center advisory committee 3-6 on August 17, with opponents arguing existing committees already provide oversight. Ozark's Planning and Zoning Commission unanimously recommended preemptive data center regulations on August 25, 2026 — requiring a conditional use permit, environmental impact report, noise compliance and size/use disclosure — which now go to the Board of Aldermen. Kirksville's Planning and Zoning Commission unanimously recommended confining data centers to a single heavy industrial district, with council action expected October 26, 2026. Pettis County enacted a temporary moratorium on large data center projects (30+ acres or $5M+) in October 2026 pending an economic and environmental study, and Wentzville's Board of Aldermen passed a six-month moratorium on October 7. Kirksville's council unanimously adopted its data center zoning ordinance the week of October 26, 2026 — confining facilities to the M-2 heavy industrial district with a 500-foot residential setback and special use permits — and Springfield's council votes November 16 on extending its administrative delay, which expires November 17, into February 2027.

name: Montana
summary: No statewide moratorium despite significant lobbying efforts, but county-level action has begun. On July 9, 2026 Missoula County commissioners approved an interim zoning moratorium of up to one year on new data centers while permanent regulations are drafted; the county separately requires data center and crypto operations to offset 100% of electrical consumption with new renewable energy. Up to 14 data centers have been proposed statewide. In Butte-Silver Bow, a district court judge is weighing a lawsuit over rejected signatures on a data center ballot initiative: the county clerk accepted 3,652 signatures on July 31, 2026 but rejected the initiative on August 10, and as of August 20 the judge had sought additional briefing with a decision expected within a week.

name: Nebraska
summary: Nebraska has significant data center activity with Google facilities in Papillion, Omaha, and Lincoln, plus new mega-proposals. Gage County's Planning & Zoning Commission unanimously recommended an 18-month moratorium on June 16, 2026, now awaiting a Board of Supervisors vote; several other Nebraska counties already have moratoriums. Broken Bow adopted a six-month moratorium on July 15, 2026, extendable by up to 12 more months. Governor Jim Pillen joined President Trump at the July 23, 2026 White House roundtable expanding the Ratepayer Protection Pledge. County-level rulemaking advanced in August 2026. Lincoln County set a timeline for finalizing data center regulations, holding a public hearing August 11 in North Platte and targeting August 31 for a final hearing on a zoning ordinance requiring closed-loop cooling, proof that infrastructure costs will not shift to ratepayers, and residential screening. Broken Bow gave first reading to an ordinance requiring noise studies, decommissioning bonds at 150% of costs, and foreign ownership disclosure. Gage County commissioners held a public hearing in early September 2026 — drawing about 30 speakers citing water, land use and property-value concerns — on extending the county's data center pause from 8 to 18 months, with a decision expected within two weeks. Kearney approved the 368 MW Project Horizon expansion in September 2026 while adopting a ten-page data center regulatory package covering water efficiency, noise, and conditional-use review.

name: Nevada
summary: Nevada, particularly the Reno-Sparks area, is a major data center market with state tax abatements for qualifying facilities. On May 14, 2026 the Reno City Council voted 6-1 for a temporary moratorium on new data center construction permits (through December 31, 2026 or until new rules are adopted) — the first Nevada local government to do so — with four pipeline projects exempted. On June 1, 2026 the Council voted 6-1 to extend the moratorium through August 31, 2027 (or until new regulations are adopted). Not all Nevada cities followed: on July 22, 2026 the Henderson City Council rejected a proposed 180-day moratorium in favor of case-by-case development agreements. Separately, Boulder City is seeking a construction stay and Interior Board of Land Appeals relief after learning the BLM authorized a data center by amending an existing 2023 solar permit rather than opening a new public review. Nevada's first countywide ban followed on August 19, 2026, when Nye County commissioners voted 5-0 to prohibit data centers in the Pahrump Valley and the Basin 162 groundwater area after a meeting that drew hundreds of attendees and more than two hours of public comment. A companion measure (No. 2026-14) establishes land-use regulations and special use permitting for data centers elsewhere in the county. On November 3, 2026, Boulder City voters rejected Question 1 — which would have added data centers as an approved use in the Eldorado Valley Transfer Area — with ~71% opposed, keeping data centers excluded from the city's land-use plan for the area.

name: New Hampshire
summary: New Hampshire's HB 1265 proposes a one-year moratorium on data center construction (public hearing held February 11, 2026), and SB 439 on municipal data center zoning authority was enacted. Governor Kelly Ayotte, after signing the pro-development off-grid electricity law HB 672 earlier in 2026, has reversed course: on September 2, 2026 she said she opposes 'putting any data center in the state of New Hampshire,' and in the week of September 7-10, 2026 she confirmed she will seek a multi-year statewide data center moratorium in her next budget, which would take effect in July 2027 unless she issues an executive order sooner. Her stated motivation: ISO-New England confirmed a large data center would raise regional energy prices. House Democrats are separately planning a 24-month moratorium bill for the 2027 session. The Republican legislative majority has now joined the shift: on September 18, 2026 Senate President Sharon Carson (R-Londonderry) announced the Senate will pursue AI data center moratorium legislation in the session beginning January 2027.

name: New Jersey
summary: New Jersey enacted its first data center ratepayer-protection law: A796/S731 (the 'Data Center Fair Share'/large-load tariff act) passed both chambers on June 30, 2026 and Governor Mikie Sherrill signed it into law on July 7, 2026 as part of a package of energy-affordability bills projected to save ratepayers over $1 billion per year. It directs the Board of Public Utilities to create a dedicated rate class and tariff for large data centers (50+ MW), requiring them to commit to paying at least 85% of projected power costs for 10 years and to post financial security so costs are not shifted to other ratepayers; the BPU has 12 months to set standards. The law follows Sherrill's May 27, 2026 comprehensive data center plan (ratepayer protection, power/water reporting, community benefit agreements). Companion bill S3379 (semi-annual water and energy reporting) remains in committee, and about 60 organizations continue to push for a stronger three-year moratorium on facilities over 20 MW. Pemberton Township became the first NJ municipality to ban data centers outright; Phillipsburg passed a final ban ordinance on April 14. On August 13, 2026 the Bayonne City Council unanimously prohibited data centers citywide and Mayor Sharon Ashe-Nadrowski signed the ordinance, making Bayonne the third New Jersey municipality with an outright ban after Pemberton Township and Phillipsburg. Municipal bans accelerated sharply in late August 2026: Stafford Township (Ordinance 2026-22) became Ocean County's first outright ban, Jackson Township followed with a 4-1 vote on August 25 (Ordinance 2026-25) citing grid, water and Pinelands concerns, and North Brunswick and East Brunswick in Middlesex County enacted bans the same week. Advocacy groups now count roughly 38 New Jersey municipalities that have blocked data centers by local ordinance — the most of any state. On August 27, 2026 Governor Sherrill signed S3379/A4096, requiring data center owners and operators to file semi-annual water and energy usage reports with the BPU for at least three years (extendable), covering total and cooling/IT energy consumption, peak daily water use, water sources and backup power — completing the second element of her four-part data center plan; the administration simultaneously issued new data center guidance for municipalities. Raritan Township reintroduced a revised data center ban ordinance in September 2026, with a public hearing set for September 15. On September 15, 2026 Assemblywoman Annette Quijano introduced A5482, the Artificial Intelligence Data Center Moratorium and Impact Study Act, which would freeze approvals, construction, expansion, subsidies and tax incentives for AI data centers over 10 MW for six months and create a 12-member study commission. Raritan Township adopted its data center ban in late September 2026, closing warehouse and flex-space workarounds while permitting small accessory server rooms. Separately, the state DEP fined the DataOne facility in Vineland $1.07 million — the largest data center enforcement action in state history — for operating 62 natural-gas generators without air pollution permits, giving the company 45 days to comply. On October 8, 2026 a Senate committee advanced S4304 (Greenstein) 4-1; the bill would bar data center developers from using NDAs or other agreements to conceal development plans and would make such agreements unenforceable under the Municipal Land Use Law. In October 2026 Millburn’s Township Committee withdrew its data center prohibition ordinance (2770-26) after the Planning Board found it inconsistent with the Master Plan, while Denville introduced an ordinance to prohibit high-intensity computing facilities, with a public hearing set for November 11. In October 2026 legislators introduced A 5663 and companion S 4659, which would require a DEP study of data center environmental impacts and prohibit construction of new data centers until the study is complete.

name: New Mexico
summary: New Mexico Democratic lawmakers have announced a statewide data center moratorium bill for the 2027 session and gave it its first public airing on August 11, 2026 before the interim Science, Technology and Telecommunications Committee. Reps. Micaela Lara Cadena (D-Mesilla) and Angelica Rubio (D-Las Cruces) told the committee the pause would let the state set parameters around data center development before more capacity is locked in; Rep. Eleanor Chávez (D-Albuquerque) is a co-sponsor and Sen. Carrie Hamblen (D-Las Cruces) is backing the proposal. The driver is Project Jupiter in Doña Ana County — the roughly 2.5 GW Oracle and OpenAI campus that is among the largest data center projects in the country. Republicans on the committee pushed back: Sen. Jay Block (R-Rio Rancho) called for a formal economic impact statement on jobs, investment and tax revenue that a moratorium would forgo. Santa Fe, Sierra and Socorro counties have already enacted local pauses. Separately, state regulators rejected a natural gas pipeline serving Project Jupiter for a second time. On August 25, 2026 the state Supreme Court paused the air-permitting process for Project Jupiter and canceled a September 14 hearing while environmental challenges over the project's water authorization and power supply are pending. In Grant County, a commissioner proposed a one-year moratorium (vote set for September 24, 2026) in response to a secretive natural gas-powered data center proposal near Hachita and Playas. The legal picture around Project Jupiter shifted in mid-September: on September 17, 2026 the state Supreme Court unanimously denied petitions from New Energy Economy and the Center for Biological Diversity and lifted the stays it imposed in August, allowing the air-quality permit proceeding (under a new hearing officer) and construction-well drilling in Santa Teresa to resume. Separately, Google announced on September 14, 2026 that it is exploring a data center in Lea County — what would be its first self-built New Mexico development. Raton's city commissioners rejected a proposed one-year moratorium 3-2 on September 22, 2026, citing existing municipal utility safeguards, despite a 477-signature resident petition opposing data centers. Grant County commissioners enacted a one-year moratorium 4-1 on October 22, 2026, barring data centers and their dedicated power, water and transmission infrastructure in unincorporated areas from November 21, 2026 through November 21, 2027.

name: New York
summary: New York now has the nation's first statewide data center moratorium, imposed by executive action. On July 14, 2026 Governor Hochul signed Executive Order No. 62, directing DEC to hold in abeyance all new and pending discretionary permits and approvals for data centers of 50 MW or greater that were not deemed complete before the order took effect. The pause runs until the Department of Public Service completes a Generic Environmental Impact Statement (GEIS) on energy demand, water use and air quality and DEC issues a findings statement — framed as up to one year. The EO also directs Empire State Development to publish a Community Investment Framework within 60 days, directs DPS to convene a Data Center Interconnection Working Group within 60 days and to consider a Grid Acceleration Fund, and requires DEC to report on water withdrawal regulations within 12 months. It exempts manufacturing, quantum and biomedical research, accredited universities and Empire AI, and medical facilities. Separately, the legislature's Responsible Data Center Development Act (S10642/A11560) — which passed both chambers on June 4, 2026 and reaches further than the EO, covering 20 MW+ facilities and adding separate utility rate classes and impact studies — had still not been delivered to or acted on by the Governor as of July 20. Hochul has until December 31, 2026 to act once it is delivered; Assembly Speaker Heastie has said he remains hopeful she will sign it, while her office has called the bill 'complicated.' Hochul has also signaled she will seek legislation repealing the state sales tax exemption for large data centers. Local pauses continue to layer on top of the state action: the Brookhaven Town Board voted unanimously on July 16, 2026 for an 18-month moratorium running to January 2028, and East Fishkill froze large projects through 2029 in early July — together putting a roughly $1 billion Long Island data center proposal in limbo. As of late August 2026 the Responsible Data Center Development Act remained unsigned; Governor Hochul has until December 31 to act once it is delivered, and her office has called the bill complicated. Her Executive Order No. 62 moratorium is in force in the meantime, and she has floated adding a decommissioning bond requirement. Genesee County has challenged the pause over its effect on the $19.5 billion Stream U.S. Data Centers project. Local governments continue to mirror the state action: the Town of Tonawanda approved a one-year moratorium in early August 2026 on data centers with peak demand of 20 MW or more. On August 24, 2026, 60 members of the Assembly and Senate, led by Assemblymember Didi Barrett and Senator Kristen Gonzalez, sent Hochul a letter urging her to sign the Responsible Data Center Development Act. Locally, Orangetown's Town Board approved a six-month moratorium on new data center and battery storage applications in late August, exempting DataBank's in-progress expansion. In Massena (St. Lawrence County), the Town Board voted 3-2 on September 17, 2026 against a proposed six-month moratorium, clearing the way for NCCS's roughly 400 MW project near the former Alcoa East plant. Buffalo's Common Council agreed on September 30, 2026 to move its proposed two-year moratorium forward with an amendment creating a nine-member task force, delaying the formal vote to mid-October, and the Town of Potsdam proposed a 12-month moratorium on large-scale data centers with a public hearing set for November 5. In early November 2026, the Town of Hamburg (Erie County) unanimously adopted a one-year moratorium on data center permits and applications while it revisits zoning, and New York City's mayor publicly urged Governor Hochul to sign the Responsible Data Center Development Act (S10642/A11560), which remains undelivered and unsigned alongside the Executive Order 62 statewide hyperscale moratorium already in force.

name: North Carolina
summary: North Carolina has no statewide moratorium bill, but local restriction has become the norm rather than the exception — more than 30 North Carolina jurisdictions have enacted temporary data center moratoriums or zoning freezes during 2026, and August brought the largest ones yet. Greensboro's City Council voted 8-0 (one recusal) on August 18, 2026 to adopt a 180-day moratorium on data centers drawing more than 10 MW, running through February 14, 2027; the council extended the pause by two months from the 120 days originally proposed after residents asked for far longer. Alamance County commissioners voted 5-0 on August 17 for a one-year moratorium on developments requiring 10 MW or more, after more than 23 residents spoke in favor at a hearing on what began as a six-month proposal; the ordinance includes interim research deadlines and requires commissioners to meet at least 30 days before it expires in August 2027. Waxhaw's board unanimously adopted a 12-month moratorium on August 10 as a proactive measure with no application pending, and Yadkin County took up a pause of its own. Statewide grid pressure in the Charlotte and Triangle regions continues to drive the debate. Not every effort succeeds — Stokes County commissioners rejected a six-month moratorium on July 13, 2026 and Engineered Land Solutions resubmitted its 'Project Delta' rezoning with design changes — but developers are also retreating: a 100,000-square-foot Raleigh facility was withdrawn in mid-August after community opposition and council skepticism. Statesville published its rationale for a proposed pause on July 24, and Fayetteville held a zoning hearing on August 10. Durham County joined the wave on August 25, with commissioners voting 4-1 for a nine-month moratorium through May 2027 on facilities over 100,000 square feet (exempting smaller closed-loop projects without diesel generators) — aligning with the city of Durham — while Davidson County commissioners rejected a six-month pause the same week, choosing to gather information instead. Charlotte's 150-day moratorium (enacted June 8, 2026) expires November 5; in September 2026 city staff recommended extending it after a study and a survey showing 78% community opposition. Statesville's City Council converted its proposal into a unanimous 180-day moratorium on September 15, 2026 (exempting the existing Compass project), Raleigh drafted a six-month moratorium with a public hearing set for October 6, and Beaufort County postponed its moratorium vote to October 5. In mid-October 2026 Elizabeth City approved an 18-month moratorium (October 12), while Guilford County commissioners delayed a proposed 180-day moratorium (Ordinance 2026-439) on October 15 after residents pushed for a longer pause — some calling for 32 months; Forsyth County commissioners rejected a moratorium of any length, citing litigation risk, and Davidson County takes up its own proposal the following week. Charlotte's council voted unanimously on October 26, 2026 to extend its data center moratorium through October 18, 2027 — roughly 11 more months beyond its original November 5 expiration — while pinning hopes on General Assembly action in 2027. The same week, Davidson County commissioners rejected a moratorium for the second time but approved data center zoning text amendments, and Fayetteville's council adopted development standards 6-4 ahead of a hearing on its own proposed moratorium. Mooresville's commissioners unanimously adopted a 12-month moratorium on new data center applications on November 2, 2026, adding Iredell County's largest town to the state's two dozen active local pauses.

name: North Dakota
summary: No statewide moratorium. Morton, Mercer, and Dunn counties retain active moratoriums on data center construction; Oliver County repealed its moratorium on May 1, 2026. A state Data Center Model Ordinance Working Group completed a model ordinance in January 2026. In early September 2026 an interim legislative committee recommended against SB 2406, a draft bill penalizing developers who enter nondisclosure agreements with public agencies, while a separate committee continues studying data center and AI policy for possible 2027 legislation. Harwood voters delivered the only pro-development result among the 41 local data center measures decided nationally on November 3, 2026, defeating (~76% opposed) a proposed independent-review requirement for large industrial projects including data centers.

name: Ohio
summary: Ohio legislators are reviewing data center energy and community impacts. In April 2026, the Ohio Ballot Board approved a statewide constitutional amendment initiative — the 'Prohibition of Construction of a Data Center' — allowing signature collection to begin. The initiative would ban data centers exceeding 25 MW; as of mid-June 2026 organizers had gathered only roughly 70,000 signatures — far short of the 413,488 valid signatures required by the July 1, 2026 deadline, so the initiative failed to qualify for the 2026 ballot; backers said they plan to resume the effort in 2027. Multiple local moratoriums remain active across Columbus-area and northeast Ohio townships. The fight has shifted to municipal ballots: on July 15, 2026 Sunbury City Council unanimously certified a citizen-initiated charter amendment to the November 3, 2026 ballot that would cap data center peak load at 25 MW — effectively blocking a planned $2 billion Amazon campus — and Pataskala residents are pursuing a similar fall vote. Columbus is drafting regulations requiring water conservation plans and developer-funded sewer upgrades. On July 24, 2026 Governor Mike DeWine signed on to the White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge, committing to keep data center utility and infrastructure costs off consumers. On August 4, 2026 Rep. Jennifer Gross introduced House Bill 983, the Data Center Accountability and Citizen Protection Act, which would require a local citizen vote before any new data center is built, set environmental standards, regulate cooling water use, and require facilities to supply their own electricity — applying retroactively to more than 150 existing Ohio data centers. In late August 2026 Pataskala's City Council unanimously rejected Aligned Data Centers' 200 MW site plan over unresolved power supply questions; a November ballot measure will ask voters whether large data centers should be permitted in the city. In early September 2026 Miamisburg's council voted 6-0 for a nine-month moratorium and Newton Falls enacted a 12-month moratorium 4-0. In September 2026, Trenton's City Council approved a November ballot initiative that would ban data centers, even as the city pursues a 601-acre annexation for an AWS campus. Mid-September brought more local pauses: Lima approved an 18-month moratorium on September 15, 2026 (exempting Google's existing facility), McDonald Village passed a one-year emergency moratorium on September 17 after a developer pitched 8-12 buildings at the former McDonald Steel site, and Piqua gave first reading to a charter amendment that would prohibit high-intensity computing uses, while Columbus proposed utility-rate, renewable-energy and decommissioning standards for large data centers with a council vote expected September 28. Fayette County commissioners approved a moratorium through June 1, 2027 covering seven townships on September 21, 2026, and Warren County commissioners — after directing their prosecutor to draft a temporary moratorium on September 22 — unanimously approved a six-month moratorium on hyperscale development (10,000+ sq ft) in county-controlled areas on September 28, 2026, pending an Ohio EPA water impact study expected in November. On October 6, 2026 Allen Township (Hancock County) trustees adopted zoning limiting data centers to I-2 districts with air cooling, a 1,250-foot residential setback, a 10,000-gallon-per-day water cap, a 40-decibel noise limit and a 10 MW load cap — while exempting data centers inside planned unit developments. In the week of October 19, 2026, Cleveland extended its moratorium on standalone data centers through January 29, 2027; Urbana's council rejected a settlement with Thor Equities (with roughly $115M in potential damages at stake) and will keep fighting the data center zoning lawsuit; and Champaign County voters will decide a data center ban measure on November 3. Heading into the November 3, 2026 election, 18 Ohio communities have data center-related measures on the ballot, including an outright ban in Hubbard and an Ashville referendum on repealing the agreement that exempts two EdgeConneX facilities from the village moratorium. Vienna Township trustees extended their moratorium a third time (180 days) in late October, and Hubbard Township trustees kept their moratorium after rejecting proposed zoning regulations as too loose. The November 3, 2026 election was a watershed: Ohio voters decided 21 local data center measures — more than any other state — and passed restrictions in nearly all of them. Full or 25 MW-threshold bans passed in Trenton (Issue 17, ~80%), Piqua (~67%), Hubbard (~77%), Sunbury (~79%), Conneaut (~65%), Defiance (~65%), Granville (~82%), Oregon (Issue 25, ~61%), Pataskala (~74%), Upper Sandusky (~77%) and Urbana (~77%). Grove City voters approved Issue 28 (~55%) requiring citywide votes on large developments, Perry Village approved Issue 16 (~87%) requiring financial guarantees from subsidized hyperscale projects, and Adams County's Monroe and Sprigg townships adopted zoning requiring data-center-compatible districts. Wilmington voters overturned four rezonings covering roughly 550 acres by ~80% margins, and Ashville voters rejected (~82% against) the referendum to uphold the village's EdgeConneX negotiation resolution. The lone pro-data-center advisory in Monroeville failed with ~88% opposed. Trenton's result blocks annexation for a planned 1,000 MW Amazon campus. With this wave of voter-enacted bans added to the state's two dozen local moratoriums, Ohio now has active restrictions across much of the state even without statewide legislation.

name: Oklahoma
summary: Governor Stitt signed HB 2992 — the Data Center Consumer Ratepayer Protection Act of 2026 — into law on May 11, 2026 (effective July 1). It requires large-load customers adding 75 MW or more (including data centers, AI facilities, and crypto miners) to sign long-term cost agreements covering their share of electricity and infrastructure rather than shifting costs to other ratepayers, and adds land-acquisition disclosure and transparency requirements. SB 1488's broader moratorium proposal stalled earlier in the session. Tulsa enacted a nine-month moratorium on new data center construction through December 2026, but Meta broke ground on a $1B+ AI-optimized data center at Fair Oaks Innovation Park in East Tulsa on April 21, 2026 — the company's first data center in Oklahoma — under an exemption for pre-approved existing projects. Oklahoma City also enacted a moratorium through end of 2026. Sand Springs faced recall efforts after rezoning for a Google data center. On August 10, 2026 Cherokee Nation Principal Chief Chuck Hoskin Jr. banned hyperscale data centers on tribally owned and trust lands, following a task force report in which 64% of nearly 1,600 tribal citizens surveyed opposed the facilities; projects on non-tribal land within the reservation boundaries now require consultation with the tribal government. In Tulsa County, Google was confirmed on August 20 as the end user behind Project Clydesdale, a 506-acre campus west of Owasso where Beale Infrastructure broke ground in October 2025, including a new substation and roughly 1.5 miles of water lines — with residents raising concerns about the rezoning process and limited public engagement. In Piedmont, residents are gathering signatures on three citizen initiative petitions targeting the 'Project Open Sky' campus — a temporary moratorium, noise standards, and a voter-approval requirement — needing 172 valid signatures each for ballot placement. In the Osage Nation, legislation introduced September 30, 2026 (ONCA 26-70) would require tribal Congress approval for hyperscale data center projects, following the Cherokee Nation's August ban on tribal and trust lands. In early October 2026, citizens of the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes voted 261-83 at the tribes' annual Tribal Council meeting to impose a three-year moratorium on data center construction on tribal lands through October 2029, citing water use and transparency concerns. Oklahoma City's council approved its first mega-data center — Beltline Energy — 6-3 on October 27, 2026, with conditions including a 75,000-gallon daily water cap, no treated water for cooling, a 55-decibel noise limit and weekday-only generator testing.

name: Oregon
summary: Oregon is implementing the 2025 POWER Act (HB 3546), under which the PUC approved a separate PGE data center tariff on July 7, 2026 (~29% increase for data centers). On September 8, 2026, Governor Tina Kotek announced a roughly one-year pause on data center development on state-owned land and in state buildings — immediately pausing unapproved requests for easements, rights-of-way, leases, rentals, land-use permits, and sales or transfers of state-owned property for data center projects, until July 1, 2027 or until statewide action directs otherwise. Kotek said the state currently lacks authority for a full statewide moratorium; advocates rallying at the Capitol are pushing for a three-year statewide pause, and moratorium legislation is planned for the 2027 session.
