Separately, Eugene rejected a data center proposal at the former Hynix plant as inconsistent with employment-focused zoning. Local action continued in mid-September: Woodburn's council unanimously approved a 120-day moratorium; Eugene staff ruled the former Hynix campus off-limits to data centers under its E-1 zoning and the city barred employees from signing data center NDAs; and on September 17, 2026 Portland's City Council unanimously passed a resolution — co-sponsored by all 12 councilors — refusing data center NDAs, requiring council notification of data center inquiries of 20 MW or more, and declaring intent to pursue a moratorium or zoning restrictions on hyperscale data centers. Salem's City Council gave final approval to a 120-day moratorium on September 22, 2026 and stood up a Data Center Task Force, with town halls in October and recommendations due in December. Hillsboro's City Council advanced permanent zoning restrictions on October 6, 2026 that would shrink land eligible for primary-use data centers from roughly 6,600 acres to 608 and require public hearings, with a final vote set for October 20; the city's moratorium remains in effect until November 24, 2026. In her most sweeping action yet, Governor Tina Kotek directed DEQ in an October 9, 2026 letter to Director Leah Feldon (reported October 13) to pause air- and water-quality permits — NPDES, WPCF, Air Contaminant Discharge and Title V — for construction or operation of new or expanding data centers until July 1, 2027, and to halt processing municipal wastewater permit renewals or modifications meant to accommodate data center discharge. The directive, which critics and industry call a de facto statewide moratorium, expands her September pause on state-land transactions and gives time to act on her Data Center Advisory Committee’s recommendations (public comment runs through October 24) ahead of possible 2027 legislation. Amazon said it was disappointed and warned the move could cost Oregon thousands of jobs and billions in planned investment. Clackamas County commissioners unanimously enacted a 120-day moratorium on data centers in unincorporated areas on October 22, 2026, effective immediately.

name: Pennsylvania
summary: Pennsylvania moved from disclosure requirements to gatekeeping in August 2026. On August 18, 2026 Governor Josh Shapiro signed Executive Order 2026-05, directing the Department of Environmental Protection to review a data center permit application only if the developer has made a legally binding commitment to the Governor's Responsible Infrastructure Development (GRID) Requirements and has already obtained local government approval. The order also removes AI data center proposals from the state's Fast Track permitting program and prohibits the use of nondisclosure agreements on data center projects. The GRID Requirements cover energy affordability, environmental protection, workforce and economic development, transparency, and community engagement; projects that accept them get expedited review, while non-compliant projects face prolonged permitting. The state has roughly 100 pending proposals and has issued only about five permits. Critics on both sides said the order falls short — of a moratorium on one side, and of predictability for developers on the other. The order builds on the first statutory regulation, enacted July 12, 2026 when Shapiro signed the $50.8B FY2026-27 budget with the substance of SB 146 and HB 1924 folded in: data centers with peak demand of 10 MW or more must file annual electricity and water reports with fines up to $10,000 per day, and the PUC gained authority to review and validate the load forecasts utilities submit to PJM. The stand-alone bills — HB 2150 (passed the House 133-68 in April), HB 2151, HB 1834, HB 2496, HB 1667 and the GRID Standards bill HB 2650 — remain stalled in the Republican-led Senate, and Sen. Katie Muth's three-year hyperscale moratorium bill is still in introduction phase. Locally, Bedford Township adopted a 20-page ordinance in early August covering setbacks, lighting, noise limits, environmental impacts and electricity use, and Pocono Township eliminated its data center overlay district in July. Locally, Doylestown Township unanimously advanced a draft ordinance in late August limiting data centers to conditional uses in light-industrial districts (adoption possible in October), and Salem Township scheduled an August 28 vote on expanding a data center overlay zone for Glenbrook Group's proposed 39-building, $1.4 billion campus. West Hempfield Township (Lancaster County) approved Ordinance 6-26 in early September 2026, limiting data center size and proximity to residential and agricultural areas. In September 2026, Springhill Township (Fayette County) moved toward a temporary ban on new data center and power-plant applications, and Clinton Township supervisors unanimously rejected Lindy Corporation's 20-building campus as environmentally unsound. Reading's Planning Commission is weighing a zoning amendment limiting data centers to heavy manufacturing districts (possible vote October 20), and Lycoming County's Planning Commission reviewed a draft curative amendment with hearings possible in mid-November. On September 29, 2026 the Senate Communications and Technology Committee unanimously approved SB 1408 (Pennycuick), which would ban NDAs between data center developers and local governments or state agencies; the bill heads to the full Senate. East Buffalo Township scheduled an October 12 public hearing on an ordinance restricting data centers to its industrial district. Separately, Kline Township supervisors unanimously approved Amazon's 350-acre data center campus (~2 million square feet) in late September. In early October 2026 the legislative push broadened: the House Energy Committee unanimously advanced HB 2775 (requiring grid interconnection applications and fees before local zoning approval) and HB 2828 (requiring data centers to bear the cost of new generation and grid upgrades), and the House Consumer Protection, Technology & Utilities Committee unanimously approved HB 2674 (barring data centers from claiming public utility status) — even as Governor Shapiro and legislative leaders rejected citizen calls for a statewide moratorium. Locally, Bethlehem's council gave 7-0 initial approval to the city's first data center zoning rules (final vote October 20), and Luzerne County's Planning Commission weighed a revised amendment loosening setback and noise limits. Concord Township closed the public hearing on its data center zoning ordinance on October 14, 2026 (possible adoption November 4), and Swatara Township commissioners approved community benefit agreements totaling $120.3 million for the proposed Highlands West and Highlands East data centers. In the week of October 19, 2026, Somerset County commissioners unanimously enacted a county data center ordinance (1,000-foot residential setbacks, noise and lighting limits), South Annville Township in Lebanon County adopted a zoning ordinance requiring decommissioning plans and a community benefits agreement, and Archbald's council unanimously denied conditional-use zoning for Cornell Realty Management's 14-building, 578-acre Wildcat Ridge hyperscale campus after nine hearings; an appeal is expected. Luzerne County Council began work in late October 2026 on an ordinance that would require a special exception from the Zoning Hearing Board for every data center in the 19 municipalities relying on county zoning, while Salem Township moved the other way, expanding its data center overlay district by more than 3,000 acres.

name: Rhode Island
summary: No statewide moratorium legislation. On May 5, 2026 the Town of Smithfield enacted a zoning ordinance banning data centers in all districts for about two years (4-1 vote), one day after Hanton City Investments filed an application for a woodland site. State legislators have introduced data center regulation bills. On August 10, 2026 the Charlestown Town Council voted 5-0 to prohibit data centers and battery energy storage systems, citing the town's reliance on well water and septic systems and the risk of contamination — the second Rhode Island town to ban data centers after Smithfield. In late August 2026 Cumberland referred a proposed data center-restricting zoning ordinance to a council subcommittee ahead of a public hearing.

name: South Carolina
summary: South Carolina's H. 5286 bars state and local governments from granting permits, approvals, or incentives for new data centers until January 2028. Covers rezoning, special use permits, building permits, and economic incentives. Filed March 2026, referred to Ways and Means. The South Carolina session has ended with the bill still in committee. County action has filled the gap: Greenwood County approved a one-year moratorium 4-3 in early July 2026 and barred data centers from industrial districts, Spartanburg County Council passed second reading of a one-year moratorium on July 21, 2026 (a third reading is still required), and McCormick County directed staff to draft a moratorium for its August 18, 2026 agenda. Spartanburg County Council delayed its final reading on the one-year moratorium on August 17, 2026, pushing the vote to September 21 to take more public input and consider broadening the pause; the $2.8 billion NorthMark project already under construction would not be affected either way. In September 2026, Jasper County approved a temporary moratorium on first reading and Mount Pleasant set debate on a 120-day moratorium targeting hyperscale loopholes in light industrial zones. Clarendon County's council gave unanimous third-reading approval to its moratorium on September 15, 2026, closing permitting loopholes while it studies environmental and community impacts. In the week of September 21, 2026, Spartanburg County passed its one-year moratorium 5-1 on final reading (with amendments exempting facilities of 65 MW or less sited in industrial parks or on former industrial sites, followed by a disputed unposted 'reconsideration' meeting), and Kershaw County unanimously passed a one-year moratorium covering data centers, crypto mining and data processing; Jasper County's moratorium had its second reading September 21. Jasper County's moratorium passed second reading September 28, 2026 (third reading pending), and Fairfield County released a timeline toward a 12-month moratorium with three town halls and a March 2027 hearing. Ahead of the 2027 session, Sen. Tom Davis is drafting a bill that would require closed-loop cooling, encourage on-site power generation and restrict where data centers can locate, and Sen. Russell Ott has suggested mandatory disclosure of projected energy and water use. The City of Newberry adopted its own 150-day moratorium on final reading November 2, 2026 — layering a municipal pause on top of Newberry County's existing 12-month moratorium — and Spartanburg County advanced development agreements for three projects (including Valara's 457 MW, $2.8 billion campus) past second reading in early November, showing the county pairing its moratorium with negotiated agreements rather than blanket refusal.

name: South Dakota
summary: South Dakota rejected moratorium bills (SB 232, HB 1301) but enacted SB 135 and HB 1038, requiring data centers with 10+ MW to pay for increased electricity rates and preserving local governments' ability to regulate. South Dakota's largest city has explicitly chosen rules over a pause: on August 20, 2026 Sioux Falls Mayor Christine Erickson said she opposes a data center moratorium, preferring clear regulatory guardrails that developers understand upfront rather than signaling the city is not open for business.

name: Tennessee
summary: No statewide moratorium legislation, but local pauses are spreading. Washington County enacted a ~15-month moratorium on data centers and crypto mines in March 2026, Johnson City adopted a one-year moratorium in the heavy industrial district and extended it to December 3, 2026, McMinnville adopted an 18-month moratorium on June 3, 2026 covering data centers, Bitcoin mining, and microchip manufacturing, and Hamilton County adopted a one-year moratorium on July 17, 2026 for rural and unincorporated areas. Counties are also tightening zoning rather than pausing outright: Coffee County voted 16-0 on July 14, 2026 to confine data centers to its M-2 Special Impact Industrial District. Crossville is weighing a two-year moratorium and Nashville residents have pressed the Metro Council for slower data center growth. Smithville enacted an 18-month moratorium on data centers and cryptocurrency mining in early August 2026, blocking permits even though no project has been proposed there. Gallatin advanced a 12-month moratorium in September 2026, with a formal vote set for mid-September. In Memphis, the City Council voted 7-5 on October 6, 2026 to postpone the final vote on the amended moratorium ordinance — a 12-month pause on large-scale data centers, with a pending amendment to extend it to 18 months — to October 20, after protests disrupted the meeting amid organized opposition to xAI's water and air impacts in South Memphis. Morristown's council is advancing zoning rules confining data centers to heavy industrial districts with 500-foot setbacks. Mid-October 2026 brought a cluster of Memphis-area actions: Millington’s Board of Mayor and Aldermen approved Resolution 44-2026 on October 12, a six-month moratorium on applications for non-grid power generation and industrial-scale computing (effective immediately, expiring April 12, 2027); a Shelby County moratorium for unincorporated areas passed first reading 5-4 the same day; and on October 20 Memphis's council rejected an 18-month moratorium on a 6-6 tie but passed a 135-day pause on data center construction and applications while siting rules are written. Rutherford County’s Regional Planning Commission unanimously recommended a 12-month moratorium on October 12, and Rogersville passed a first-reading ordinance 4-2 confining data centers to its industrial district. With Hamilton County’s and Smithville’s moratoriums and now Millington’s in force, local restrictions are active in the state. Montgomery County commissioners approved strict data center limits 17-4 on October 19, 2026, raising residential setbacks to 500 feet, capping site sizes and noise, and requiring applicants to prove water and power capacity.

name: Texas
summary: Texas escalated to a full statewide permitting freeze. On September 21, 2026 Governor Abbott directed the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to halt issuance of all permits for data center projects statewide until ERCOT completes its grid audit (expected mid-December 2026), expanding the pause beyond grid interconnection to environmental permitting; the directive states no state agency shall proceed with regulatory approvals related to data center development until the ERCOT and Texas Water Development Board audits are complete, and it applies even to fully 'islanded' facilities relying on behind-the-meter generation. TCEQ must report compliance to the Governor's office by October 19, 2026. Texas now has an effective statewide pause on new data center grid connections. On August 3, 2026 Governor Greg Abbott directed the Public Utility Commission of Texas and ERCOT to conduct a comprehensive verification and audit of every data center advancing through ERCOT's interconnection queue, and ERCOT halted its 'batch zero' large-load transmission planning study (which reviews requests of 75 MW or more) until the review concludes. State officials say roughly 250-300 projects representing about 200 GW of requested demand — more than twice ERCOT's all-time peak — are covered, and that the audit will take several months; developers must disclose state financial assistance, power and water use projections, generation sources, ownership, and community impact mitigation. Projects outside ERCOT or relying purely on behind-the-meter generation may fall outside the directive. Local action accelerated in parallel. On June 16, 2026 the San Marcos City Council voted 4-3 to make data centers ineligible in every zoning district — the first outright municipal ban in Texas — a move State Sen. Paul Bettencourt says exceeds the city's authority under Texas preemption law. Fort Worth's City Council voted unanimously on August 11, 2026 to begin a 90-day moratorium and a three-part regulatory plan including an 11-member Data Center and Infrastructure Commission, with findings due November 3 and a final vote set for February 16, 2027. Keller voted unanimously on August 19 to sue neighboring Westlake over a 1.1 million-square-foot facility sited 506 feet from Keller homes and to start its own 90-day moratorium. El Paso County commissioners approved a resolution on August 18 asking the state for a development pause and expanded county authority, and Austin scheduled a council work session for August 25 on siting, water, noise and lighting rules. Hill County's May 2026 county moratorium was rescinded in June after a developer sued for more than $100 million, and Tom Green County abandoned its own effort in response — a reminder that county-level pauses remain legally fragile in Texas. In Lubbock, the city accepted a citizen petition on August 26 for an 18-month moratorium on high-water, high-energy data centers, with a September 8 public hearing and a 30-day window for the council to adopt or reject it. Austin held a council work session August 25 on siting, water, noise and lighting rules. Lubbock's council passed a nonbinding resolution in September 2026 pledging to hold off on large-scale data centers pending new rules, with a petition-led 18-month moratorium vote set for late September. On September 14, 2026 Governor Abbott directed the Texas Water Development Board to penalize data centers and other large water users that failed to file mandatory water-use surveys — only about 28% of data centers responded over three years — with consequences including permit ineligibility, referral to prosecutors and possible bars on utility connections. In October the statewide freeze showed enforcement gaps: TCEQ issued an air permit on October 13, 2026 to Sitespan LLC for a data center project between San Antonio and Seguin despite the Governor's pause, then suspended it after public scrutiny and said it is shutting down its automatic filing system to review data center applications manually. Separately, Arlington staff proposed zoning options that would confine stand-alone data centers to industrial districts with specific use permits, a 300-foot residential setback and a ban on evaporative cooling. The November 3, 2026 election added a political dimension to the statewide freeze: Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who won the governorship, has pledged to keep data center approvals paused until the Legislature passes ratepayer and water protections when it convenes in January 2027, meaning Abbott's agency-level permitting pause is likely to persist or expand through the transition.

name: Utah
summary: Utah offers tax incentives for data center development and has seen significant growth in the Salt Lake City area, but local pushback has begun: on May 26, 2026 Iron County approved a 180-day moratorium on new data center and related power-plant applications (the Pronghorn project is exempt, the Red Butte project paused).

name: Vermont
summary: Governor Phil Scott vetoed H.727, the Sustainable Data Center Deployment Act, on May 28, 2026, citing existing Act 250, Public Utility Commission, and municipal zoning authority. The bill had passed with tripartisan support (Senate 26-3, near-unanimous House voice vote) and would have required utility contracts insulating other ratepayers from large-data-center costs, additional site analysis, and climate-fund payments. Lawmakers voted 83-52 to override on May 28 — six votes short of the 90 needed. Vermont's S.205 (100 MW+ AI data center moratorium through July 2030) remained in committee. Governor Scott was also one of only three governors — with Florida's DeSantis and New Hampshire's Ayotte — who declined to sign the White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge when it was expanded on July 23, 2026.

name: Virginia
summary: Virginia's HB 1515 moratorium was carried over to the 2027 session (effectively dead for 2026), and HB 2084 directing the SCC to review data center rate classifications was enacted. The months-long budget standoff over the roughly $1.6 billion data center sales tax exemption ended in late June: the General Assembly passed a ~$205 billion biennial budget on June 22, 2026 (Senate 23-16, House 71-22) that retained the exemption but added a first-of-its-kind energy consumption tax on data centers of $0.011 per kWh consumed monthly, capped at $600 million per year to the general fund. Governor Spanberger proposed budget amendments — including new water-conservation requirements for future data centers — which the legislature approved on June 29, and she signed the budget on June 30, 2026, ending the impasse before the July 1 fiscal deadline. Virginia remains the world's largest data center market. Local activity continued into late July: on July 21, 2026 Loudoun County asked the State Corporation Commission to stay its approval of a Dominion Energy transmission line while settlement talks with Dominion and the school system proceed, and on July 22 the Pittsylvania County Board approved a resolution supporting STACK Infrastructure's $100 billion Berry Hill megasite campus — roughly 2,990 acres to be built out over 15 to 30 years. In a July 31, 2026 order made public in early August, the State Corporation Commission ruled that large-load data centers must pay for transmission facilities built solely to serve them — costs previously spread across all customers through the Rider T-1 line item — resolving a dispute over roughly $1.5 billion in Dominion Energy transmission spending and cutting the average residential monthly increase from about $2.90 to $0.94. Dominion has 90 days to file a new cost-assignment proposal. Local restriction also hardened: Chesapeake's City Council unanimously approved a zoning ordinance on August 19, 2026 limiting data centers to conditional uses in industrial zones, banning groundwater use, closing by-right development loopholes and removing the Fentress Overlay exception, with an eight-month application pause still in effect and nearly 40 residents testifying. Loudoun County supervisors voted 6-1 in July to draft a temporary moratorium, with a vote set for September 15, while Amazon filed a by-right site plan for four buildings on the former GWU campus to bypass planning commission review. In Franklin County, the Project Flash campus was cancelled in mid-August after developer negotiations failed amid opposition from more than 40 speakers. Henry County adopted a strict Data Center District ordinance on August 25, 2026, requiring rezoning plus a special use permit, 1,000-foot setbacks from non-industrial properties, a 50 dBA noise limit, closed-loop cooling only, and mandatory water-use studies. In September 2026, Christiansburg's Town Council voted 6-0 to require conditional use permits for all data centers, ending by-right status in industrial zones. Prince William County's Planning Commission voted on September 10, 2026 to recommend ending by-right data center development — requiring special use permits with public hearings and shrinking the data center overlay district — ahead of a September 22 Board of Supervisors hearing, and Loudoun supervisors are preparing amendments to pause new applications and eliminate by-right permitting, with debate expected October 6. On September 22, 2026 the Prince William County Board of Supervisors voted 8-0 to end by-right data center development countywide — facilities outside designated opportunity zones now need Special Use Permits, and the overlay district shrinks from about 9,700 acres to roughly 3,641 — a landmark shift in one of the state's largest data center markets. Chesterfield County deferred for a second time (to November 18) a vote on using data center tax revenue to cut the county's car tax. On September 18, 2026 Governor Spanberger signed Executive Order 22 establishing a Data Center Accountability Framework, directing state agencies to develop evaluation tools and designating the Eastern Virginia Groundwater Management Area (including Suffolk) as a cooling water scarcity area. Suffolk's Planning Commission voted 8-0 in mid-September to recommend prohibiting data centers as a primary use in all zoning districts, with a City Council vote set for October 21. In October 2026 Sen. Russet Perry (D-Loudoun), joined by Sen. Danica Roem, prefiled SB 843 for the 2027 session: a three-year statewide moratorium that would bar localities, DEQ and the State Corporation Commission from approving data center building permits — and distribution lines or on-site power serving only data centers — from July 1, 2027 until July 2030, to give lawmakers time to write rules for the industry. Gov. Spanberger has not backed a moratorium, pointing instead to her Data Center Accountability Framework (EO 22); more moratorium bills are expected before the January session. Loudoun County supervisors deferred to November 17, 2026 a vote on a 12-month pause on data center and substation applications (retroactive to September 15 and covering 33 pending applications), after the county attorney advised a full moratorium would not be legal.

name: Washington
summary: Washington enacted SB 5982 requiring large data center customers to meet the same clean energy deadlines as utilities and directing the UTC to establish reporting requirements. HB 2515 — a broader data center regulation bill — passed the House 51-41 but died in the Senate after Microsoft and other tech companies opposed it. Local activity has accelerated dramatically: Seattle Councilmembers Juarez, Lin, and Council President Hollingsworth introduced a 365-day emergency moratorium on new large (10 MW+) data centers; the Council passed the emergency ~1-year moratorium 9-0 on June 9, 2026, and Spokane followed with its own one-year citywide moratorium (6-1) on June 23. Two developers had withdrawn Seattle expansion plans amid the backlash, and Mayor Wilson announced parallel administrative steps on May 1. In late July 2026 Spokane County proposed extending the pause to unincorporated areas with a nine-month building permit moratorium expiring after the 2027 legislative session. Spokane County commissioners unanimously approved a four-month moratorium on new data center permits on August 19, 2026 — trimmed from an earlier nine-month proposal — to let staff draft zoning regulations, with the option to extend depending on the outcome of commission elections. Yakima County commissioners unanimously directed staff on August 4 to draft a six-month moratorium after residents raised water scarcity concerns, despite no applications pending. Port Angeles' council voted 5-1 in early September 2026 to direct staff to draft a six-month moratorium on new data center applications. Lincoln County held the required public hearing on October 5, 2026 for its six-month emergency moratorium on data centers and battery energy storage. West Richland's council restricted data centers to Mixed-Use Light Industrial zones on November 3, 2026, after a proposed six-month moratorium fell short (three of five votes needed). AWS is meanwhile proceeding with its first Washington data center campus — the 300 MW, three-building Attalia campus at Wallula Gap Business Park in Walla Walla County — now in State Environmental Policy Act review.

name: West Virginia
summary: West Virginia offers tax incentives for data center development and is marketing its low energy costs to attract facilities.

name: Wisconsin
summary: The Wisconsin 2025-26 legislature ended its session without passing a statewide data center bill: a GOP ratepayer/water-protection measure (AB 840) passed the Assembly 53-44 but died in the Senate, and a Democratic 'very large customer' rate-class bill did not advance. Local action continues to accelerate — Dodge County adopted an 18-month moratorium in early June 2026 (29-2), and the Sheboygan Common Council passed a moratorium on zoning and building permits for data centers over 10,000 square feet on July 23, 2026 — joining Port Washington's first-in-the-nation anti-data-center referendum ban and moratoria in Madison, Manitowoc County, and Driftless Area townships. Local pauses kept spreading in August 2026. La Crosse's Plan Commission advanced an 18-month moratorium on August 3, with a public hearing August 5 and a Common Council vote August 13, and Bellevue's village board voted unanimously on August 10 for a one-year moratorium extendable by six months — joining nearby Wrightstown and Manitowoc County. Opposition also grew to two natural gas plants proposed to power data centers in Kenosha and Walworth counties, after a UW-Madison study estimated $1.38 billion in nationwide health harms over their 30-year lifetimes. In late September 2026 Madison unveiled a draft zoning framework (100,000-square-foot building cap, hyperscale excluded, 1,000-foot facility separation; council vote expected January 2027), and Manitowoc County finalized a 24-page draft permanent ordinance capping developments at under 500 acres ahead of a County Board hearing. On October 13, 2026 Milwaukee’s Common Council unanimously approved a one-year moratorium on new data center development and expansions while the city drafts permanent zoning rules, which would ban facilities over 60,000 square feet and confine smaller ones to industrial-heavy zones. In mid-October 2026, Wisconsin Rapids enacted a one-year moratorium and rejected 7-0 a permit for PNK Group's proposed hyperscale center; the DNR settled a Sierra Club lawsuit over Vantage's Port Washington campus on October 16 by agreeing to a statewide strategic analysis of AI data center environmental impacts (final by January 2028); and Republican legislators circulated a bill to eliminate the state's data center sales tax exemption, which Democratic leaders dismissed as unlikely to move this session. Janesville voters approved a referendum on November 3, 2026 (~63% yes) requiring a citywide vote before the city commits to the proposed GM/JATCO data center site if its cost exceeds $450 million.

name: Wyoming
summary: Wyoming has taken no statewide legislative action to restrict data centers and remains generally favorable to large-load development, but local governments have begun to engage. Cheyenne rejected a proposed moratorium in May 2026. In late July 2026, Park County commissioners proposed requiring special-use permits for data centers and other heavy electrical-load users as part of the county's first land-use overhaul in more than a decade, despite no project having been proposed there. The state also hosts the planned 1,250 MW Prometheus Hyperscale campus. Cheyenne's City Council annexed and zoned a 34.46-acre parcel on August 10, 2026 as a staging area for North Range Business Park data center construction, over resident objections about aquifers, noise and incremental annexation; a citizen petition drive on data center limits neared its signature threshold in early August. On September 1, 2026 Laramie County commissioners approved a Planned Unit Development zone change for Vantage Data Centers' 'Project Latigo,' a $20 billion, 1,835-acre campus south of Cheyenne with on-site natural gas generation and closed-loop cooling, projected to create up to 2,000 jobs.
